nameStory: The Horn-faced Mason Bee gets its name from the distinctive horn-like projections that stick out from its lower face, giving it an almost medieval armored appearance. These facial 'horns' are unique among New England bees and make this species instantly recognizable once you know what to look for.
description: The Horn-faced Mason Bee is a solitary bee originally from Northern Asia that has made its way to New England. Unlike honeybees that live in large colonies, each female works alone to build her own nest and raise her young. These medium-sized bees are excellent pollinators and are known for being quite gentle - they're much less likely to sting than other bee species, even when disturbed.

idTips.label: Facial horns
idTips.description: Look for the telltale horn-like projections extending from the lower part of the face - they feel rigid if you examine a specimen and are unique among New England bees

idTips.label: Solitary behavior
idTips.description: Watch for individual bees working alone rather than in groups, often seen visiting flowers methodically one by one

idTips.label: Docile nature
idTips.description: Notice how calm and non-aggressive these bees are - they'll often continue foraging even when you're observing them closely

idTips.label: Mason bee build
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a robust, compact body typical of mason bees - stockier than honeybees but not as fuzzy as bumblebees

idTips.label: Nesting sites
idTips.description: Look for them investigating small holes in wood, stems, or man-made structures where they collect mud to build their nest chambers

habitat: Horn-faced Mason Bees can be found in gardens, parks, orchards, and woodland edges throughout New England where flowering plants are abundant. They're particularly drawn to areas with both good flower resources and suitable nesting sites like hollow plant stems, beetle holes in wood, or even bee houses put up by gardeners. You'll often spot them in suburban areas where they've adapted well to human landscapes.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and are most active, busily collecting pollen and nectar while building their nests in available cavities.
seasonality.summer: Adults complete their reproductive cycle and die off, while their offspring develop inside sealed nest chambers.
seasonality.fall: Young bees are fully developed but remain dormant in their nest cells, preparing for winter.
seasonality.winter: New generation overwinters as fully formed adults inside their sealed nest chambers, waiting for spring warmth.

funFact: This bee was accidentally introduced from Asia and has become such an effective early-season pollinator that some orchardists now actively encourage them - they can start working in cooler spring weather when honeybees are still huddled in their hives!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other mason bees, but the facial horns are a dead giveaway - no other mason bee in New England has these distinctive projections. Remember: horns on the face = Horn-faced Mason Bee.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being a non-native species, Horn-faced Mason Bees are generally welcomed by gardeners and farmers because they're such efficient, gentle pollinators and don't compete aggressively with native species.
compareHints: Among New England's mason bees, the Horn-faced Mason Bee is the only one with facial horns, making identification straightforward. The Blue Orchard Bee is more metallic in color, while the Maine Blueberry Bee is darker overall, but neither has the characteristic facial projections that make this species unmistakable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's mason bees, the bufflehead stands out primarily due to its enlarged head structure.

Among New England's mason bees, the Blue Orchard Bee is distinguished by its intense metallic blue coloration - most other Osmia species are darker black, brownish, or have less pronounced metallic sheens.
Among New England's mason bees, the Taurus Mason Bee can be distinguished from the more common Blue Orchard Bee by its darker coloration and lack of metallic blue-green sheen.
